title: The evolution of green finance research: A comprehensive bibliometric analysis.
paragraphs: Green finance has gained increasing attention from industries, academics, and policymakers due to its critical role in balancing environmental sustainability with economic development. It plays a crucial role in addressing climate change and fostering the transition to a low-carbon economy [ 1 ]. Given its broad scope, green finance draws insights from multiple disciplines, e.g. bank [ 2 ], economics [ 3 ], investment [ 4 , 5 ], social security [ 6 ], environment [ 3 , 7 ], monetary policies [ 8 , 9 ], and regulations [ 10 , 11 ]. Publications on green finance have been increasing extensively. For example, sovereign environmental, social, and governance [ 12 , 13 ], Green banking and environmental performance [ 14 ], Financial development and renewable energy [ 15 ], economic policy uncertainty and renewable energy [ 16 ], green bond and energy prices [ 17 ], renewable energy and CO2 emission [ 18 ], and environmental sustainability, globalization and, hydroelectricity consumption [ 19 ]. Despite its growth, a comprehensive analysis of the trends, key contributors, and research gaps in the field remains necessary to understand its evolution and gaps for further exploration.

A comprehensive understanding of the global trends and frontiers in green finance research is crucial for identifying research status quo, emerging topics, knowledge gaps, and informing future research directions. By systematically exploring the existing literature, the article shows the overall growth of publications and citations, the distribution of disciplines, the geographical distribution of publications, impactful contributors, i.e. authors, institutions, countries/regions, and their collaboration networks, and the evolution of research topics and trends over time. The article seeks to enhance comprehension of the current state of green finance research and offer valuable insights for future directions and industry applications in the field.

Understanding the global evolution of green finance research holds significance for several reasons. First, it reveals the current global landscape of research in this domain. Second, it aids in pinpointing knowledge gaps for future exploration. Third, it enables the identification of emerging topics, allowing researchers to stay ahead in the field. Fourth, this understanding offers valuable insights for choosing future research directions in the green finance field.

Following a bibliometrics, the following research questions are explroed [ 20 ]. Why a comprehensive review on green finance research is needed? Why is green finance research relevant and interesting? What are the patterns of publications and citations in green finance research? What are the impactful countries/regions, institutions, researchers in the green finance research. What are the collaboration networks in green finance research? What are the influential articles and who are the influential authors in green finance research? What are the co-citation patterns and main thematic topics within the field of green finance research? What are the intellectual structures in green finance research? What are the emerging topics in green finance research? How the research topics evolve over time? How might the findings inform emerging topics and future research directions in the evolving green finance research?

The article contributes to the literature by conducting a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of 1923 articles in the green finance field. First, it provides a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of 1923 articles, offering an extensive and detailed overview of the field. The article presents a visualized summary of publication and citation patterns, which can serve as a valuable resource for researchers, policymakers, and investors. Second, it traces the evolution and current state of green finance research. Third, the article examines key aspects of the field, including publication trends, disciplinary classifications, journal distribution, influential authors, and collaboration networks. Co-citation analysis is used to uncover pivotal research clusters, landmark and pivot nodes, and dynamic topics, thereby offering a thematic mapping of the field's development. The article contributes to the understanding of the evolution, trend patterns, and future research directions in green finance research, providing valuable insights for researchers, investors, practitioners, and regulators.

The literature commonly explores various topics in green finance. For example, the definition of green finance [ 1 ], overview of green finance research [ 2 , [1] , [1] , [1] ], green finance and its impact on economic development or environmental quality [ 24 , 25 ], policy and regulations [ 26 , 27 ]. Literature further investigates the green finance markets, e.g. green bonds and green stocks [ [1] , [1] , [1] ], the relationships between technological innovations and green finance [ 31 , 32 ], sustainable finance and financial institutions [ [1] , [1] , [1] ], circular economy [ 36 ], taxation [ 37 , 38 ], digital currencies [ [1] , [1] , [1] ], central banking and green finance [ 42 ].

Bibliometric analysis is first introduced by Pritchard [ 43 ]. It has been widely used to investigate emerging trends and the evolution of scientific fields. For example, blockchain [ 44 ], quantitative finance [ 45 ], energy system [ 46 ], artificial intelligence [ 47 ], central bank digital currencies [ 48 ], gender, work and organization [ 49 ], Bitcoin [ 50 ],etc.

The field of green finance has gained significant attention in recent years. Zhang, Zhang [ 22 ] summarizes the current state and development trends of green finance based on a dataset of 381 articles from 2001 to 2018. Akomea-Frimpong, Adeabah [ 2 ] explore research on green finance in the banking sector, focusing on products and determinants, based on 79 articles. The findings assist banks in adopting and developing green finance initiatives. Bhatnagar and Sharma [ 51 ] conduct a bibliometric analysis of the growth and evolution of the concept of green finance and identifies its enablers using 666 articles. They point out that green finance is in a nascent stage in developing countries, and green bonds are the most popular tool adopted for green financing. Akomea-Frimpong, Adeabah [ 2 ] focus on 46 article related to green finance. Naeem, Karim [ 52 ] employ a dataset of 1413 articles sourced from Scopus to assess the present status and prospective trends within the realm of green and sustainable finance. Debrah, Darko [ 53 ] examine 1125 articles in green finance using a mixed-methods systematic review. This article contributes to the literature by conducting a thorough bibliometric analysis, offering valuable insights into the global landscape and evolution of research in the green finance field.

To examine the global trends in green finance research, this article collects data from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoS), a widely recognized and comprehensive database of high-impact academic publications. The search was conducted using the following query formula: TS = (“green financ∗" OR “climate financ∗" OR “carbon financ∗" OR “sustainable financ∗" OR “environment financ∗"), where the asterisk (∗) accounts for different variations of the root terms. This approach ensures that the dataset captures the breadth of green finance research across various forms and terminologies.

Four refinement steps are applied. First, article, proceeding paper, and early access article types are selected. Second, the time span is set from 1992 to 2022. Third, duplicate records are removed using the CiteSpace function. Fourth, plural forms of keywords are replaced with singular forms. The final dataset includes 1923 publications on green finance (downloaded on March 1, 2023). This dataset represents a robust and diverse collection of green finance research from around the world.

Quantitative approaches, i.e. statistical analysis and bibliometrics are applied in the article. The article starts with a statistical analysis to explore the dataset, which provides an overview of the constituents, e.g. authors, institutions, countries, and their contributions and growth within the green finance field. The article then proceeds with bibliometrics, which is a commonly used approach to gain insights into the development of the intellectual structure and identify emerging trends in a research field [ 54 ]. The main techniques of bibliometric analysis include co-citation analysis, co-authorship analysis, keywords co-occurrence, bursts, and clustering [ 55 ].

Apart from bibliometrics, other techniques for conducting a systematical review include altmetrics, patent analysis, meta-analysis, text mining, computational literature reviews. This article applies bibliometrics due to its common usage for analyzing research evolutions in different fields, its explanatory power, and its inherent capacity to systematically map and analyze extensive publications. The authors apply bibliometrics due to the extensive volume of articles in green finance, amounting to 1923 publications in this article. Conducting a systematic literature review individually for such an extensive dataset would be practically impractical. This approach aligns with the article's objective of providing a comprehensive overview on green finance research.

Fig. 1 illustrates the trend of publications and citations on green finance spanning from 1992 to 2022. The first publication is Feitelson [ 56 ], which discusses economic instruments for sustainable finance. Publications and citations on green finance remain comparatively low from 1992 to 2008, with less than ten articles per year. From 2009 onwards, publications and citations related to green finance show a noticeable increase. Notably, the number of publications reaches 109 in 2018. This upward trend continued in 2021 and 2022, with 393 publications and 4949 citations, and 678 publications and 11,294 citations, respectively. The rise in publications and citations on green finance since 2009, particularly in 2021 and 2022, reflects the growing academic interest and recognition of its importance in sustainable development and climate action. The top three disciplines are Environmental Studies, Environmental Sciences and Green Sustainable Science Technology, accounting for 29.69 %, 18.05 % and 31.62 % of the total publications, respectively. The distribution of green finance publications across disciplines highlights the field's interdisciplinary nature, with a dominant focus on environmental sciences, while also reflecting the growing importance of integrating economic, financial, and business perspectives to address sustainability challenges within financial systems and public policies. Table 2 lists the top ten cited articles in green finance from the dataset, based on total citations within the dataset. Taghizadeh-Hesary and Yoshino [ 57 ] propose two frameworks for encouraging private participation in green finance and investment. They suggest the establishment of green credit guarantee schemes and returning a portion of tax revenue from green energy supply spillover effects to investors. Campiglio [ 58 ] highlights that commercial banks may not respond as expected to price signals and may hesitate to lend to low-carbon activities. The article argues that additional policies, e.g. monetary policies and macroprudential financial regulation, are necessary to incentivize banks to direct credit towards low-carbon sectors, beyond carbon pricing. Zhang, Mohsin [ 59 ] investigate the relationship between public spending on research and development (R&D) and green economic growth and energy efficiency in Belt and Road Initiative. They emphasize the importance of public spending on R&D in driving green economic growth and energy efficiency. Flammer [ 60 ] focuses on corporate green bonds and finds that issuing green bonds can credibly signal a company's commitment to environmental sustainability. The top cited articles discuss various topics, e.g. private participation, banking and monetary policy, public spending, corporate green bonds, green total factor productivity, demand for green finance, blue carbon projects, and financial inclusion. The top-cited articles in green finance reveal a broad and multifaceted approach to addressing the challenges of sustainable finance, highlighting key themes such as private sector involvement, the need for regulatory frameworks, the role of public investment in driving green growth, and the signaling power of green bonds, underscoring the complexity of aligning financial systems with environmental sustainability goals. The co-citation analysis reveals that, first, green bonds and credit policies are central themes in green finance, demonstrating the field's focus on creating financial products that support sustainability goals. Second, central banks and financial regulators are increasingly viewed as key players in shaping green finance strategies, reflecting a shift from market-driven initiatives to policy-supported frameworks. Third, increasing research examines the application of green finance in emerging markets, suggesting a broader, more inclusive global approach to sustainability. The analysis of co-cited articles in green finance reveals distinct, well-defined research clusters, with high homogeneity within each, and underscores the dynamic nature of green finance as an evolving field, particularly through the recent prominence of green bonds and the active exploration of policy mechanisms like green credit and carbon emissions reduction.

Three pivot nodes in green finance are Taghizadeh-Hesary and Yoshino [ 57 ], Bumpus and Liverman [ 77 ], and Bowen [ 82 ]. Taghizadeh-Hesary and Yoshino [ 57 ] examine ways to encourage private involvement in green finance and investment. They suggest the implementation of a green credit guarantee scheme and returning a fraction of tax revenue generated from green energy supply to investors as means to minimize the risk of green finance and maximize the rate of return of green energy projects. Bumpus and Liverman [ 77 ] analyzes the governance structures of the Kyoto Protocol's Clean Development Mechanism and unregulated voluntary carbon offsets. They emphasize the dissimilarities in the regulation and complexity of the carbon reduction chain. Bowen [ 82 ] explores the principles that should be followed when attempting to raise funds for climate action in developing nations. According to his analysis, private finance could have a significant impact if a universally implemented emissions pricing system were put in place. The identification of landmark and pivot nodes in green finance not only highlights the foundational works that have shaped the field but also underscores the pivotal connections between disparate research areas, suggesting a dynamic and evolving landscape where key articles act as bridges that drive interdisciplinary integration and innovation, especially in addressing the complex challenges of climate finance and private sector involvement.

The article identifies three emerging areas for future green finance research: green energy, green technology/innovation, carbon emissions and digital economy. First, one emerging topic in green energy is smart grid systems, investigating the integration of digital technologies to enhance the efficiency and reliability of energy distribution networks. Additionally, research delving into how artificial intelligence can optimize energy production, storage, consumption, and management. Second, emerging topics at the intersection of green technology/innovation and green finance encompass several areas. For example, the development of innovative financial instruments to support green finance, sustainable infrastructures development, green building technologies, and the role of financial innovations in promoting green development across industries. Third, the development of carbon pricing mechanisms, the incentives and risks associated with carbon-intensive industries, green bonds and financial instruments that specifically target carbon reduction initiatives. Furthermore, the role of financial institutions and central banks in supporting carbon reduction goals is also a hot topic. Fourth, researchers are delving into the implications of digital economy on green finance. The focus includes the environmental impact of data centers, cloud computing, and the overall energy consumption of digital infrastructure, the rise of digital currencies with a focus on environmental sustainability, how new technology like blockchain can enhance transparency and traceability in green investments.

The authors encourage interdisciplinary and international collaborations between the green finance field and other fields, e.g. economics, business, finance, energy, management, investment, and environmental studies. One avenue for future research is how innovations in financial instruments support green development and green finance. How to measure the environmental and social impacts of investments related to green finance, and how to encourage various stakeholders, e.g. individuals, firms, financial institutions, etc. To contribute to sustainable development. Future research may explore how policies and regulatory frameworks can be improved to incentivize green finance investments, and what role governments or central banks play in fostering a green financial ecosystem. Researchers could apply a global perspective, exploring how different countries and areas approach green finance, the impact of international collaborations, and the potential for global standards in green finance.

One limitation of this study is its reliance on a dataset of 1923 articles sourced exclusively from the Web of Science Core Collection. Future research could broaden the scope by incorporating publications from additional databases, such as Scopus and patent repositories, to capture a more comprehensive range of scholarly and technological advancements. Another limitation is the nature of bibliometric analysis itself, particularly the challenges posed by science mapping techniques. These methods may not fully capture the latest research, as newly published articles often take time to gain recognition within the academic community. To address this, future studies could leverage artificial intelligence technologies to monitor emerging publications in real-time, enabling more timely and dynamic analysis of trends in green finance. While bibliometric analysis is effective in identifying broad patterns of growth and collaboration, it does not provide in-depth insights into the specific methodologies or theoretical frameworks employed within individual articles. To overcome this limitation, future research could incorporate complementary approaches such as meta-analysis, case studies, interviews, and content analysis, which would provide a deeper understanding of the underlying dynamics in green finance. These diverse methodologies would offer a more nuanced perspective, capturing the complexities and evolving nature of the field.

The findings of this article suggest several policy implications for the advancement of green finance. First, fostering interdisciplinary and international collaboration between green finance and sectors such as energy, economics, and environmental studies is essential to developing comprehensive solutions for sustainable development. Second, policies may prioritize incentives for investment in emerging areas such as green energy, technological innovation, carbon pricing, and the digital economy. Integrating financial instruments like green bonds and carbon pricing mechanisms into regulatory frameworks is critical to mobilizing capital for these sectors. Third, the role of governments and central banks in creating a supportive green financial ecosystem through targeted policies and incentives is beneficial. Additionally, enhancing the measurement of environmental and social impacts of green finance will improve transparency and accountability.

This article presents a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of green finance research using 1923 articles collected from the Web of Science Core Collection. Various aspects of green finance research are discussed, e.g. publications, citations, discipline categories, journal distributions, highly cited articles, highly cited publications, collaboration networks at the levels of authors, institutions, countries or regions. Science mapping is applied to identify co-citation clusters, landmark nodes, pivot nodes, and top cited authors within the dataset. Topic trends in green finance are analyzed through the time zone view of keyword co-occurrence and keyword burst. By highlighting key contributors in green finance research and offering an overview of the field, this article contributes to a deeper understanding of the domain of green finance.

Second, the top three highly cited publications within the dataset are Taghizadeh-Hesary and Yoshino [ 57 ], Campiglio [ 58 ], and Zhang, Mohsin [ 59 ]. The most productive authors in green finance are Farhad Taghizadeh-Hesary, Muhammad Mohsin, J. Timmons Roberts, Liu, Zhen, Sadiq, Muhammad Siddik, and Abu Bakkar. Third, the main clusters of co-cited articles in green finance are contributor state, green bond, green finance, central bank, local communities, green credit policy, alternative role, green bond, mitigating carbon emission, current debate, blue carbon, dryland, and environmental performance. The five typical landmark nodes in green finance filed are Buchner, Clark [ 67 ], Pickering, Betzold [ 68 ], Wang and Zhi [ 69 ], Zhou, Tang [ 70 ], and Yu, Wu [ 62 ]. The three pivot nodes in green finance filed are Taghizadeh-Hesary and Yoshino [ 57 ], Bumpus and Liverman [ 77 ], and Bowen [ 82 ]. Fourth, the three fundamental keywords in green finance filed are green finance, climate finance, and sustainable finance. Other keywords with highest co-occurrence include climate change, sustainable development, green bonds, sustainability, and renewable energy.

The evolution of the green finance research field can be divided into three stages. i.e. carbon finance and carbon markets (2008–2010), climate finance, climate change, and climate policy (2011–2017), and sustainable development goals and financial development (2018–2022). The four emerging areas in green finance are green energy, green technology/innovation, carbon emissions and digital economy.

The findings have significant implications for scholars, policymakers, and professionals seeking a deeper comprehension of the current state and evolution of green finance research. The article contributes both theoretically and practically to the green finance field. Green finance has gained increasing attention from industries, academics, and policymakers due to its critical role in balancing environmental sustainability with economic development. It plays a crucial role in addressing climate change and fostering the transition to a low-carbon economy [ 1 ]. Given its broad scope, green finance draws insights from multiple disciplines, e.g. bank [ 2 ], economics [ 3 ], investment [ 4 , 5 ], social security [ 6 ], environment [ 3 , 7 ], monetary policies [ 8 , 9 ], and regulations [ 10 , 11 ]. Publications on green finance have been increasing extensively. For example, sovereign environmental, social, and governance [ 12 , 13 ], Green banking and environmental performance [ 14 ], Financial development and renewable energy [ 15 ], economic policy uncertainty and renewable energy [ 16 ], green bond and energy prices [ 17 ], renewable energy and CO2 emission [ 18 ], and environmental sustainability, globalization and, hydroelectricity consumption [ 19 ]. Despite its growth, a comprehensive analysis of the trends, key contributors, and research gaps in the field remains necessary to understand its evolution and gaps for further exploration.

A comprehensive understanding of the global trends and frontiers in green finance research is crucial for identifying research status quo, emerging topics, knowledge gaps, and informing future research directions. By systematically exploring the existing literature, the article shows the overall growth of publications and citations, the distribution of disciplines, the geographical distribution of publications, impactful contributors, i.e. authors, institutions, countries/regions, and their collaboration networks, and the evolution of research topics and trends over time. The article seeks to enhance comprehension of the current state of green finance research and offer valuable insights for future directions and industry applications in the field.

Understanding the global evolution of green finance research holds significance for several reasons. First, it reveals the current global landscape of research in this domain. Second, it aids in pinpointing knowledge gaps for future exploration. Third, it enables the identification of emerging topics, allowing researchers to stay ahead in the field. Fourth, this understanding offers valuable insights for choosing future research directions in the green finance field.

To examine the global trends in green finance research, this article collects data from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoS), a widely recognized and comprehensive database of high-impact academic publications. The search was conducted using the following query formula: TS = (“green financ∗" OR “climate financ∗" OR “carbon financ∗" OR “sustainable financ∗" OR “environment financ∗"), where the asterisk (∗) accounts for different variations of the root terms. This approach ensures that the dataset captures the breadth of green finance research across various forms and terminologies.

Four refinement steps are applied. First, article, proceeding paper, and early access article types are selected. Second, the time span is set from 1992 to 2022. Third, duplicate records are removed using the CiteSpace function. Fourth, plural forms of keywords are replaced with singular forms. The final dataset includes 1923 publications on green finance (downloaded on March 1, 2023). This dataset represents a robust and diverse collection of green finance research from around the world.

Quantitative approaches, i.e. statistical analysis and bibliometrics are applied in the article. The article starts with a statistical analysis to explore the dataset, which provides an overview of the constituents, e.g. authors, institutions, countries, and their contributions and growth within the green finance field. The article then proceeds with bibliometrics, which is a commonly used approach to gain insights into the development of the intellectual structure and identify emerging trends in a research field [ 54 ]. The main techniques of bibliometric analysis include co-citation analysis, co-authorship analysis, keywords co-occurrence, bursts, and clustering [ 55 ].

Apart from bibliometrics, other techniques for conducting a systematical review include altmetrics, patent analysis, meta-analysis, text mining, computational literature reviews. This article applies bibliometrics due to its common usage for analyzing research evolutions in different fields, its explanatory power, and its inherent capacity to systematically map and analyze extensive publications. The authors apply bibliometrics due to the extensive volume of articles in green finance, amounting to 1923 publications in this article. Conducting a systematic literature review individually for such an extensive dataset would be practically impractical. This approach aligns with the article's objective of providing a comprehensive overview on green finance research.

The article identifies three emerging areas for future green finance research: green energy, green technology/innovation, carbon emissions and digital economy. First, one emerging topic in green energy is smart grid systems, investigating the integration of digital technologies to enhance the efficiency and reliability of energy distribution networks. Additionally, research delving into how artificial intelligence can optimize energy production, storage, consumption, and management. Second, emerging topics at the intersection of green technology/innovation and green finance encompass several areas. For example, the development of innovative financial instruments to support green finance, sustainable infrastructures development, green building technologies, and the role of financial innovations in promoting green development across industries. Third, the development of carbon pricing mechanisms, the incentives and risks associated with carbon-intensive industries, green bonds and financial instruments that specifically target carbon reduction initiatives. Furthermore, the role of financial institutions and central banks in supporting carbon reduction goals is also a hot topic. Fourth, researchers are delving into the implications of digital economy on green finance. The focus includes the environmental impact of data centers, cloud computing, and the overall energy consumption of digital infrastructure, the rise of digital currencies with a focus on environmental sustainability, how new technology like blockchain can enhance transparency and traceability in green investments.

The authors encourage interdisciplinary and international collaborations between the green finance field and other fields, e.g. economics, business, finance, energy, management, investment, and environmental studies. One avenue for future research is how innovations in financial instruments support green development and green finance. How to measure the environmental and social impacts of investments related to green finance, and how to encourage various stakeholders, e.g. individuals, firms, financial institutions, etc. To contribute to sustainable development. Future research may explore how policies and regulatory frameworks can be improved to incentivize green finance investments, and what role governments or central banks play in fostering a green financial ecosystem. Researchers could apply a global perspective, exploring how different countries and areas approach green finance, the impact of international collaborations, and the potential for global standards in green finance.

One limitation of this study is its reliance on a dataset of 1923 articles sourced exclusively from the Web of Science Core Collection. Future research could broaden the scope by incorporating publications from additional databases, such as Scopus and patent repositories, to capture a more comprehensive range of scholarly and technological advancements. Another limitation is the nature of bibliometric analysis itself, particularly the challenges posed by science mapping techniques. These methods may not fully capture the latest research, as newly published articles often take time to gain recognition within the academic community. To address this, future studies could leverage artificial intelligence technologies to monitor emerging publications in real-time, enabling more timely and dynamic analysis of trends in green finance. While bibliometric analysis is effective in identifying broad patterns of growth and collaboration, it does not provide in-depth insights into the specific methodologies or theoretical frameworks employed within individual articles. To overcome this limitation, future research could incorporate complementary approaches such as meta-analysis, case studies, interviews, and content analysis, which would provide a deeper understanding of the underlying dynamics in green finance. These diverse methodologies would offer a more nuanced perspective, capturing the complexities and evolving nature of the field.

The findings of this article suggest several policy implications for the advancement of green finance. First, fostering interdisciplinary and international collaboration between green finance and sectors such as energy, economics, and environmental studies is essential to developing comprehensive solutions for sustainable development. Second, policies may prioritize incentives for investment in emerging areas such as green energy, technological innovation, carbon pricing, and the digital economy. Integrating financial instruments like green bonds and carbon pricing mechanisms into regulatory frameworks is critical to mobilizing capital for these sectors. Third, the role of governments and central banks in creating a supportive green financial ecosystem through targeted policies and incentives is beneficial. Additionally, enhancing the measurement of environmental and social impacts of green finance will improve transparency and accountability.

This article presents a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of green finance research using 1923 articles collected from the Web of Science Core Collection. Various aspects of green finance research are discussed, e.g. publications, citations, discipline categories, journal distributions, highly cited articles, highly cited publications, collaboration networks at the levels of authors, institutions, countries or regions. Science mapping is applied to identify co-citation clusters, landmark nodes, pivot nodes, and top cited authors within the dataset. Topic trends in green finance are analyzed through the time zone view of keyword co-occurrence and keyword burst. By highlighting key contributors in green finance research and offering an overview of the field, this article contributes to a deeper understanding of the domain of green finance.
